step: The Loss Distribution Is Not the Audit Report
statement: The bug classes that get the most audit attention are not the ones that lose the most money.

step: Containment When There Is No Undo
statement: On-chain you cannot reverse the theft, so incident response is entirely about bounding what has not happened yet.

step: The Researcher With a Universal Jailbreak
statement: Disclosure is a relationship under time pressure, and the party that behaves predictably controls the outcome.

step: Break It, Then Guard It, in Foundry
statement: You do not understand a vulnerability until you have written the exploit that proves it and the test that proves the fix.

step: Day Thirty-One: The Incident You Did Not Build The Program For
statement: In your first month you have no credibility to spend, so spend process instead.

step: The Security Ladder and the Honest Cost of Each Rung
statement: Security levels are only useful if each rung is defined by the attacker it stops, not by the controls it contains.

step: Build Two-Party Control That Survives Friday Afternoon
statement: Two-party control fails not when it is attacked but when it is inconvenient, so design it against inconvenience.

step: Lab: The Authorisation Bug No Scanner Will Ever Name
statement: Broken object level authorisation is invisible to tools because a correct response and a catastrophic one are byte-identical in shape.

step: Shift Left Was Half An Idea
statement: Moving detection earlier without moving remediation capacity earlier just relocates the queue and calls it progress.

step: Four Ways A Chain Breaks
statement: Almost every open source compromise of the last two years reduces to phishing, a privileged automated trigger, a stolen long-lived credential, or a handover of control — and each has a different defence.

step: Break It, Then Guard It, in Foundry
statement: You do not understand a vulnerability until you have written the exploit that proves it and the test that proves the fix.

step: Exchange-Grade Custody and the Insider You Cannot Audit
statement: Hot, warm, and cold segmentation stops the outside attacker; only dual control and least privilege stop the one you hired.

step: The Job As It Actually Is
statement: The CISO is a translator, a portfolio manager, and an organisational designer who occasionally does security.

step: What A Board Can Actually Do
statement: A board has four levers and none of them is technical, so every ask must be shaped to fit one.

step: Security As A Product Organisation
statement: Turn every control you would have mandated into a product someone chooses, then measure adoption instead of compliance.

step: Availability Is a Security Property When Downtime Costs Collateral
statement: On this network your uptime is enforced by the protocol, so an availability incident and a security incident have the same shape, the same clock, and often the same cause.

step: The Distributed Hash Table Knows What You Want
statement: Every lookup you make in a public DHT is a signed confession of interest broadcast to strangers, and the strangers are cheap to become.

step: Field: Stand Up the Detection Guild
statement: The repository, the review gate and the owner are the program; everything else is content that flows through them.

step: Summiting the Pyramid: How Hard Is Your Analytic to Evade
statement: Two detections for the same technique can differ by an order of magnitude in how easily an adversary defeats them, and until you score that difference you are counting rules rather than measuring defence.

step: Delay Is the Dominant Failure Mode
statement: Most security programs are not under-resourced; they are over-delayed, and the two look identical from the outside.

step: STRIDE Applied to Boundaries, Not Boxes
statement: STRIDE is a checklist against security properties, and it only works when you point it at an interaction rather than at a component.

step: Lab: Calibrate Yourself, Then Model the Loss
statement: You are overconfident by a measurable amount, and until you measure it every number you give a board is a guess wearing a suit.

step: Four Business Days and the Word Material
statement: The SEC clock does not start when you detect an incident; it starts when you determine it is material, and the duty is to make that determination without unreasonable delay.

step: Break Glass at 02:40
statement: Break-glass access is not an exception to your controls; it is a control with its own design, its own alarm and its own rehearsal schedule.

step: What the Adversary Learns From You
statement: Every action you take is telemetry the adversary receives, and the cheapest way to lose an incident is to announce that you have found it.

step: Atoms — Identity Without a Registrar
statement: An atom is not a record you own; it is a name the network derives from your data, and derivation means nobody can gatekeep it and nobody can take it away.

step: THE VALIDATOR SESSION
statement: A region of a public knowledge graph is an asset with no owner, which means it is audited by whoever decides to audit it — and the ritual below is how a professional decides.

step: The Asset Is a File
statement: The most valuable thing your organisation owns is a set of floating point numbers, and everything about your security programme should be rearranged around that fact.

step: Egress Is the Control That Fits the Asset
statement: You cannot stop a legitimate user from reading the weights, so make it impossible for them to move the weights quietly.

step: The Engineer Who Resigned On Tuesday
statement: Insider response is the one discipline where the fastest visible action is almost always the worst one.

step: Your Perimeter Runs Through Someone Else's Datacentre
statement: The weights are decrypted in the memory of hardware you do not own, in a building you have never entered, on a chip whose firmware you did not write.

step: The Top Ten as a Coverage Map, Not a Design
statement: A shared taxonomy is worth adopting even when it is imperfect, because it makes disagreement specific.

step: Safety Failure or Security Failure
statement: If the harmed party is the user themselves, it is a safety problem; if the harmed party is someone else, it is a security problem, and the difference decides who gets paged.

step: Poisoning Does Not Scale With Your Corpus
statement: The intuition that a bigger training set dilutes an attacker's contribution is wrong, and it is the most load-bearing wrong intuition in AI security.

step: Your API Is a Side Channel
statement: Every convenience you expose in an inference API — logprobs, logit bias, deterministic sampling, verbose errors — is an oracle someone will query systematically.

step: The Instruction That Arrived As Pixels
statement: Any channel the model can perceive is an instruction channel, including the ones your threat model calls attachments.

step: Six Patterns, and the Price of Each
statement: Every real defence against injection buys security by removing capability, and the engineering skill is choosing which capability you did not need.

step: Six Patterns, and the Price of Each
statement: Every real defence against injection buys security by removing capability, and the engineering skill is choosing which capability you did not need.

step: Reviewing a Connector Ecosystem
statement: A tool description is executable text that nobody reviews, delivered by a server nobody vetted, running with credentials nobody scoped.

step: Delegation That Attenuates
statement: Authority must narrow as it passes down a chain of agents, and the default in every system you will inherit is that it widens.

step: Oversight That Is Not a Reflex
statement: A human in the loop who approves in three seconds is not oversight; they are a latency cost that legal mistook for a control.

step: The Agent Inventory Nobody Has
statement: You cannot govern agents you cannot list, and every organisation has more of them than its architecture diagram admits.

step: Three Places It Works, Three Places It Hurts
statement: A language model is excellent at compressing evidence into language and terrible at deciding what is true, so let it write and never let it conclude.

step: Detection Authoring With a Test Harness
statement: A model-drafted detection is a hypothesis; the harness that tests it against real data is the actual deliverable.

step: The Alert That Closed Itself
statement: When an automated conclusion cites evidence that does not exist, the defect is not the model — it is that your pipeline accepted an unverifiable claim.

step: The Same Capability Points Both Ways
statement: AI-assisted vulnerability research favours whoever can act on its output fastest, and that is a patching question before it is a research question.

step: Measure the Tool You Bought
statement: Any AI security capability you cannot measure against labelled ground truth over time is a vendor claim you are storing in production.

step: Measure the Tool You Bought
statement: Any AI security capability you cannot measure against labelled ground truth over time is a vendor claim you are storing in production.

step: The Frameworks You Will Be Held To
statement: Map your controls to the frameworks once, properly, and you will spend the next three years answering questions instead of rebuilding evidence.

step: An Evaluation Is a Control, Not a Report
statement: An evaluation only becomes a security control at the moment a result is bound in advance to an action nobody can talk their way out of.

step: Pre-Commitment as a Control
statement: The purpose of a capability threshold is to make a decision now that your future self, under commercial pressure, will not be able to argue away.

step: Alignment and Control Are Different Bets
statement: Alignment is a bet that the system wants what you want; control is a bet that it does not matter what it wants — a security leader funds the second and hopes for the first.

step: The Board Asks How Exposed We Are
statement: A board does not want your risk assessment; it wants to know which decisions are theirs and what happens if they choose wrongly.

step: The Researcher With a Universal Jailbreak
statement: Disclosure is a relationship under time pressure, and the party that behaves predictably controls the outcome.

step: The Class, Not The Instance
statement: Every ticket you close is one instance; every condition you change is every instance, forever.

step: The Top Ten Is A Census, Not A Threat Model
statement: The OWASP Top 10 tells you what testers found in the applications that agreed to be measured; it does not tell you what will be used against you.

step: Memory Safety: The Only Class We Know How To Delete
statement: Memory unsafety is the one major vulnerability class with a proven industrial cure, and the cure is not a rewrite.

step: Lab: SSRF Into The Metadata Service
statement: In cloud environments server-side request forgery is not an information leak, it is a credential handoff.

step: Threat Modelling Inside The Design Review
statement: A threat model is not a document; it is a forty-minute argument held before the code exists, and its only artefact worth keeping is the decisions it changed.

step: Drill: The Gate And The Release Train
statement: The moment your control blocks revenue is the moment you discover whether you designed it or inherited it.

step: Council: A Champions Network That Does Not Decay
statement: A security champions programme is a distribution network for judgement, and every one that fails does so because it distributed tasks instead.

step: The False Positive Is An Economic Instrument
statement: A tool's precision is not a technical specification; it is the exchange rate between your programme and your engineers' trust.

step: Drill: The Report Lands Two Days Before Launch
statement: A penetration test report is an input to a decision, not the decision — and treating it as the decision is how security teams get removed from the process.

step: Field: Continuous Fuzzing With Honest Coverage
statement: Claiming a project is fuzzed without publishing its coverage is the assurance equivalent of a green dashboard nobody validated.

step: xz-utils: How To Buy A Maintainer
statement: The most sophisticated supply chain attack yet documented did not exploit a single vulnerability; it exploited the fact that critical infrastructure is maintained by exhausted volunteers.

step: Lab: Harden The Pipeline
statement: Your CI system holds credentials to everything you own, executes arbitrary code by design, and is usually the least monitored production system in the company.

step: Lab: Sign, Attest, Verify
statement: An artefact you cannot trace back to a specific commit built by a specific workflow is an artefact you are choosing to trust on faith.

step: Severity Is Not Priority
statement: CVSS describes the bug in the abstract; priority is a statement about your system, your adversaries and your capacity, and only you can make it.

step: Drill: The 9.8 And The 6.5
statement: The moment you have capacity for one of two vulnerabilities is the moment your prioritisation model is either real or decorative.

step: Council: How To Say No To A Scanner Report
statement: A no you can defend in writing is a security control; a no delivered verbally in a meeting is a liability with your name on it.

step: Field: Publish A Standard With Teeth
statement: A vulnerability management standard that does not specify enforcement, exceptions and evidence is a wish list with a document number.

step: Council: The Board Asks If We Are Exposed
statement: A board does not want your findings count; it wants to know whether you would recognise the day this goes wrong, and what happens next.

step: Access Control, Proxy Slots, and the Signature You Can Replay
statement: The quiet bugs — a missing modifier, a colliding storage slot, a domain separator left off — move more money than the loud ones.

step: The Job As It Actually Is
statement: The CISO is a translator, a portfolio manager, and an organisational designer who occasionally does security.

step: The First Ninety Days That Actually Work
statement: Spend the first ninety days buying information and one credible artifact, not shipping wins.

step: The Listening Tour That Surfaces Real Risk
statement: Ask questions that only a specific person can answer, and the risk register writes itself.

step: Ground Truth: Finding Out What Is Actually There
statement: Every inherited program has a stated posture and an actual posture, and the gap lives in the denominator.

step: The Mandate Memo: Converting A Title Into Authority
statement: Authority that is not written down does not exist on the day you need it.

step: What A Board Can Actually Do
statement: A board has four levers and none of them is technical, so every ask must be shaped to fit one.

step: The Three-Slide Standard
statement: Risk narrative beats control inventory, because a narrative contains a decision and an inventory does not.
